claims.claim: Randall states that in the passage narrating Darien's death in The Darkest Road the sentences are short and the description concrete.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: Sentences are short, description is concrete.

claims.claim: Randall describes the tone of that same Darien death passage as matter-of-fact.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: The tone, moreover, is matter-of-fact.

claims.claim: Randall reads the passage narrating the departure of Arthur, Lancelot and Guinevere as a deliberate reach for rhetorical high style, in contrast with the plain Darien passage.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: the language here is an obvious attempt at rhetorical

claims.claim: Randall explains the elevated register of the Arthurian departure scene as a consequence of who perceives it, not of the event's importance.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: because it is perceived by minds capable of comprehending magnificence

claims.claim: Randall counts twenty-six different agents of focalization in The Fionavar Tapestry.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: employs twenty-six different agents of focalization
claims.page: opening section, before 'Assimilating the Secondary World'

claims.claim: Randall counts twenty-one shifts of focalization in the eighth chapter of The Summer Tree.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: shifts focalization twenty-one times

claims.claim: Randall counts eighty-seven shifts of focalization across Darien's search for Rakoth, with Darien himself the focalizant only nine of those times.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: the narrative shifts focalization eighty-seven times

claims.claim: Randall argues that Kay's shifts of focalization delay the unfolding of the story as well as advancing it.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: the shifts delay the unfolding of the story

claims.claim: Randall argues the reader must assemble Kay's secondary world by inference from the successive focalizations rather than from direct exposition.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: Our task is to piece together the world by understanding the focalizations.

claims.claim: James Gunn writes that Kay's novels stand out for their richness of character and fullness of scene.
claims.source: James Gunn, Easton Press introduction to Tigana, 30 July 1998
claims.quote: richness of character, their fullness of scene
claims.page: introduction, paragraph beginning 'That describes Tigana as well.'

claims.claim: Gunn says Tigana reads like a richly tapestried historical novel dense with character and detail.
claims.source: James Gunn, Easton Press introduction to Tigana, 30 July 1998
claims.quote: dense with character and detail

claims.claim: Gunn credits Kay's willingness to kill major characters with giving Tigana the edge of reality against what might otherwise be airily fantastic.
claims.source: James Gunn, Easton Press introduction to Tigana, 30 July 1998
claims.quote: gives the edge of reality to what might otherwise be airily fantastic

claims.claim: Cobb argues that the enrichment Kay's historical fantasy offers its readers is primarily emotional rather than rational.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, Foundation (Summer 2005)
claims.quote: primarily emotional rather than rational

claims.claim: Cobb states that in Tigana the past cannot be changed but history, meaning the memory and the record of the past, can be changed.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, Foundation (Summer 2005)
claims.quote: the past cannot be changed, but history

claims.claim: Janeen Webb characterises the plotting of A Song for Arbonne as political survival ungarlanded by personal myth, in contrast to Tigana.
claims.source: Janeen Webb, critic, The New York Review of Science Fiction
claims.quote: political survival ungarlanded by personal myth
claims.page: section comparing Tigana and A Song for Arbonne

claims.claim: Rettino argues that Kay's narrator at times sounds like a historian because of the distance at which it relates events.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, McGill honours thesis (2012)
claims.quote: whose voice at times resembles that of a historian in its distanced relation of events
claims.page: section on Tigana and the club-story

claims.claim: Rettino reads the narrator of Under Heaven as presenting himself as one Kitan historian among many.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, McGill honours thesis (2012)
claims.quote: The narrator presents himself as one Kitan historian among many.

claims.claim: Rettino observes that Kay slides world information into a character's thoughts, disguising the narrator's exposition as Jehane's thinking in The Lions of Al-Rassan.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, McGill honours thesis (2012)
claims.quote: The narrator subtly offers information to the reader, disguising it as Jehane
claims.page: section on The Lions of Al-Rassan

claims.feature: other: competing memories of one event
claims.claim: Kay says he wrote several scenes in Children of Earth and Sky in which one conversation is described by more than one of its participants.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, Los Angeles Review of Books
claims.quote: as described by more than one of the people in the conversation
claims.page: answer on multiple points of view

claims.feature: other: competing memories of one event
claims.claim: Kay says that when he switches to another character's point of view the same conversation is not the same conversation.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, Los Angeles Review of Books
claims.quote: the conversation isn’t the same. It bears a resemblance
claims.page: answer on multiple points of view

claims.claim: Kay says one starting point of Children of Earth and Sky was that it takes place on the borderlands in the lives of not-powerful people.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, Los Angeles Review of Books
claims.quote: in the lives of not-powerful people
claims.page: answer on ghosts and family legacies

claims.claim: Kay offers as an example of art outlasting power a forgotten emperor whose chronicler is remembered.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, Los Angeles Review of Books
claims.quote: a forgotten emperor and the chronicler of the reign is remembered
claims.page: answer on art enduring after empires fall

claims.claim: Pugar says Kay's narrator names places in Tigana without explaining where they are, which makes the reading feel like a historical text with geographical references.
claims.source: Petra Pugar, University of Zagreb, Words to Works
claims.quote: creates a feeling of reading a historical text with geographical references
claims.page: p. 168, section 'Geographical map as a paratext'

claims.claim: Pugar argues that Tigana's prologue persuades the reader they are reading a true account giving evidence of the past.
claims.source: Petra Pugar, University of Zagreb, Words to Works
claims.quote: they are dealing with a true account, giving evidence of the past

claims.claim: Töyrylä says Kay uses a matter-of-fact style to describe a dramatic and violent event in Tigana.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, BA thesis, University of Helsinki (2017)
claims.quote: Again a matter-of-fact style is used to describe a dramatic and violent event

claims.claim: Töyrylä describes that passage's narrator as merely reporting what happened without any commentary.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, BA thesis, University of Helsinki (2017)
claims.quote: the narrator is merely reporting what happened, without any commentary

claims.claim: Töyrylä reads the phrase 'according to most reports later' as the narrator restricting his omniscience to what people hear about the incident afterwards.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, BA thesis, University of Helsinki (2017)
claims.quote: narrating only what people hear about the incident afterwards

claims.claim: Töyrylä argues that a shift out of a character's perspective is what lets Kay describe that character's execution matter-of-factly.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, BA thesis, University of Helsinki (2017)
claims.quote: enables the matter-of-fact description of his execution

claims.claim: Töyrylä argues that Kay's narrator describes things as an inhabitant of the storyworld would rather than as an outsider.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, BA thesis, University of Helsinki (2017)
claims.quote: the narrator describes things like an inhabitant of that world would

claims.claim: Töyrylä finds that in passages using the phrase 'as everyone knows' the narrator's perspective coincides with that of an average citizen of the Palm.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, BA thesis, University of Helsinki (2017)
claims.quote: concurs with that of an average citizen of the Palm

claims.claim: Hatch argues that through the historian Pertennius Kay shows the historian's power outlasting that of the world's rulers.
claims.source: Jillian Hatch, University of Calgary undergraduate paper
claims.quote: the power of the historian is more lasting than that of the rulers of the world

claims.claim: Hatch reports that the narrator of Sailing to Sarantium claims on its first page that writers of history often seek the dramatic over the truth.
claims.source: Jillian Hatch, University of Calgary undergraduate paper, quoting Kay's Sailing to Sarantium p. 1
claims.quote: writers of history often seek the dramatic over the truth

claims.claim: Kleander counts twenty-one separate focalizants and more than 150 separate focalizations in Tigana, apart from the non-focalized narrative.
claims.source: Anya Kleander, Honours dissertation, University of Stirling (2008)
claims.quote: there are twenty-one separate focalizants in Tigana, and more than 150 separate focalizations

claims.claim: Kleander reports Kay as believing that the quiet, steady accumulation of detail and complexity reaches readers almost subliminally.
claims.source: Anya Kleander (2008) quoting Guy Gavriel Kay in an SF Site interview, 2000
claims.quote: quiet, steady accumulation of detail and complexity
claims.confidence: medium — the words are Kay's, reached at second hand through Kleander's citation of an SF Site interview I did not fetch

claims.claim: Kay says he looks for the unwritten histories and the people at the margins of history.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay interviewed in Locus, 12 May 2025
claims.quote: the people at the margins of history

claims.claim: Kay says he also loves the chronicles of the dukes and the popes, alongside the unwritten lives of women and of the poor.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay interviewed in Locus, 12 May 2025
claims.quote: lives of women, and of the poor

claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun argues that the restoration of Tigana's name remains marked by loss, fragmentation and incomplete knowledge.
claims.source: Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, Orbis Litterarum (2026)
claims.quote: it remains marked by loss, fragmentation, and incomplete knowledge
claims.confidence: medium — abstract only, the article text was not reachable

claims.claim: Johnston argues that Kay's reimagined ancient and medieval settings estrange the familiar, rendering it unheimlich.
claims.source: Susan A. Johnston, in Canadian Science Fiction, Fantasy, and Horror (Palgrave Macmillan, 2019)
claims.quote: estranging the familiar, rendering it unheimlich
